blocks.text: When someone says a car has a "2.0 litre engine", they're talking about **displacement**: how much space all the pistons sweep through on one stroke.

Each cylinder is a tube. The volume one piston sweeps is the area of the tube's circle times how far the piston travels. The width of the tube is the **bore**, and how far the piston travels is the **stroke length**.

blocks.say: Volume equals pi over four, times bore squared, times stroke. With a bore and stroke of eight point six centimetres, that's about five hundred cubic centimetres per cylinder. Four cylinders gives two thousand, which is two litres.

blocks.text: When the piston is at the top, there's still a small pocket of space left above it. That's the **clearance volume** (Vc). The **compression ratio** compares the space at the bottom with the space at the top.

blocks.say: Compression ratio equals swept volume plus clearance volume, divided by clearance volume. With five hundred and fifty, that's five hundred and fifty divided by fifty, which is eleven to one.

blocks.caption: Drag the ratio. Watch the gas get crowded and the pressure climb.
blocks.narration: Drag the ratio slider. A higher ratio leaves less room at the top, so the same gas gets squeezed harder, hotter and to a higher pressure.

blocks.title: Higher = more efficient…
blocks.text: A harder squeeze gets more push out of the same fuel. That's why engineers keep pushing compression ratios up.

blocks.title: …until it knocks
blocks.text: Squeeze too hard and the mix gets so hot it lights **by itself**, before the spark, with a sharp pinging sound called **knock**. Knock can wreck pistons. Higher-octane (premium) fuel resists it, which is why high-compression engines ask for premium.

blocks.title: Diesels
blocks.text: Diesel engines use knock on purpose. They squeeze plain air to around 15–20 : 1, until it's hot enough to light fuel sprayed in at the top. No spark plug needed.
